questions.question: Describe South Africa's three-part topography and classify slopes by shape, explaining why this country is dominated by dramatic slopes.
questions.expected_answer: South Africa's surface consists of the interior plateau, a high flat erosion surface mostly between 1 200 and 1 800 metres taking in the Highveld, Free State plains and Karoo basin; the Great Escarpment, the near-continuous rim where the plateau breaks toward the coast, at its highest in the KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg above 3 000 metres and continuing through ranges like the Nuweveldberge and the Mpumalanga escarpment; and the marginal or coastal zone between escarpment and sea, including the folded Cape ranges and the east coast lowlands. Slopes dominate because the plateau supplies gentle surfaces, the escarpment drops one to two kilometres over a few horizontal kilometres — rivers like the Tugela plunge nearly 950 metres off the rim — and the marginal zone is a staircase of terraces and ranges that every coast-to-interior route must climb. Slopes are classified by shape: convex slopes bulge outward and steepen downhill; concave slopes hollow inward and are gentlest at the base; rectilinear slopes hold one constant angle; and most real hillsides are compound combinations of these stacked downhill.

questions.question: Name and characterise the four slope elements in order, and explain slope retreat, contrasting parallel retreat with slope decline and stating why South African conditions favour retreat.
questions.expected_answer: From the top down: the crest or summit is gently convex, thinly covered, slowly rounded by weathering; the cliff, scarp or free face is the steepest element, bare bedrock formed where a resistant band outcrops, called the free face because rock loosened from it falls away immediately; the talus or debris slope below is rectilinear because loose fragments settle at their angle of repose, roughly 25 to 35 degrees, with coarser blocks resting lower down after rolling furthest; and the pediment is a gently concave bedrock surface under about 5 degrees, thinly veneered with sediment, crossed by sheetwash and merging with the plain. Not every slope carries all four — without a resistant band there is no cliff. In slope retreat, the cliff sheds rock and retreats backward, the talus follows, and the pediment extends; in parallel retreat, the account Lester King built on South African landscapes, the profile keeps its proportions while relocating backward, and merging pediments eventually form a pediplain dotted with koppies and inselbergs. The alternative, slope decline, sees the whole profile flatten and round through down wasting, which suits humid, deep-soiled regions. South Africa's resistant caprocks, semi-arid climate and sparse vegetation keep cliffs sharp and strip debris efficiently, so parallel retreat dominates and our landscapes keep sharp profiles for tens of millions of years.

questions.question: Explain spatial and spectral resolution, the vector data types with attribute data, and the raster model, showing how a GIS applies them to slope analysis.
questions.expected_answer: Spatial resolution is the size of the ground area represented by one pixel of an image — a 10-metre resolution shows fields and roads but not vehicles, and finer resolution reveals smaller detail. Spectral resolution is the number and narrowness of the wavelength bands a sensor records — visible, near-infrared, thermal — and more, narrower bands let analysts distinguish healthy veld, drought-stressed crops, bare soil and water by their different reflectance. Vector data stores discrete objects as geometry: points for single-position features like boreholes or trig beacons, lines for linear features like rivers, roads and contours, and areas or polygons for features with extent like farms, dams or districts; each object carries attribute data, the table of facts about it such as a borehole's depth and yield. Raster data lays a grid of equal cells over the land with a value in every cell — elevation in a digital elevation model or reflectance in an image — and suits continuously varying phenomena like altitude and rainfall, while vector suits sharp-edged objects. Applied to slopes, a raster elevation model lets the GIS compute a slope-angle map for a whole region at once, vector contours, farm boundaries and roads overlay it, and combining slope, soil and rainfall layers maps hillsides too steep to plough or prone to erosion — the analysis used by soil conservation and road planning departments.
